name: offline-first
context: An application treats the copy of the data on the user's device as the primary copy, not a cache of a server's. Reads and writes hit local storage and never wait for a network round trip; a background sync layer reconciles the local replica with other devices and with the server when a connection exists. The decisive statement is not that servers are absent but that their role changes — from source of truth to a supporting participant in replication. The seven ideals that define the pattern are: no spinners, multi-device, offline, multi-user, long-term preservation, security and privacy by default, and the user retaining ultimate ownership and control.
benefits: User interaction never blocks on the network — writes apply locally and the local write is the state, so there is no separate 'optimistic' mode
The application keeps functioning normally regardless of network status rather than showing an offline error that blocks work
Data ownership moves to the user; a server outage degrades collaboration, not the user's access to their own work
Conflict resolution can be automated with CRDTs, so most concurrent edits merge without user intervention or a server round trip
End-to-end encryption becomes practical because servers only ever hold ciphertext they cannot read
tradeoffs: There is no single authoritative database, so server-side authorisation, validation and auditing must be rebuilt elsewhere
Clients cannot display data they have not yet received — every new query has a first-result loading period
Sync engines carry real complexity: hybrid logical clocks, durable operation logs, retries, coalescing and idempotent application
Conflict resolution that is purely structural cannot understand domain meaning, so some conflicts still need human judgement
Replicated metadata and retained history grow over time and need compaction and garbage collection
use_cases: Collaborative editors and whiteboards where several users work and reconnect constantly
Field-service and survey applications used in areas with no connectivity
Note-taking and task applications where losing network access must not lose work
Design tools with multi-device sessions across laptop, tablet and phone
Any application that wants to keep working after the vendor shuts the backend down
avoid_when: The data is inherently non-shareable or the product requires a single canonical server record for everyone
Strong server-side authorisation is the primary control and cannot be deferred to a client replica
Multi-region write conflict resolution has not been decided — local-first pushes that decision to the front
The application is a thin client over a server whose latency is already acceptable
component_types: Local replica: the primary store on the device, typically SQLite, IndexedDB or an embedded engine
Sync engine: background component that exchanges changes with peers and the server
Operation log: durable, ordered record of local changes awaiting propagation
Conflict resolution: CRDT merge, or field-level last-writer-wins under a hybrid logical clock
Sync transport: server relay, WebSocket, or peer-to-peer such as WebRTC, local WiFi or Bluetooth
Subscription/filter model: per-client declarations of which data to mirror
anti_patterns: Building 'offline support' as an error path: showing an offline banner and blocking the user's work
Keeping the server as the source of truth and bolting a retry queue in front of it — the pattern is the inverted ownership, not the queue
Resolving conflicts by wall-clock time alone, which is non-deterministic across devices with skewed clocks
Treating a sync conflict as an exception path instead of as normal convergent state
Assuming a replica can show data it has never received, and designing the UI around that assumption
design_principles: The local copy is primary; servers hold secondary copies in a supporting role
Reads and writes never block on the network
Convergence is the default conflict policy; user resolution is the exception
Replication is transport-agnostic — a server, a peer, or a local network
The user owns the data and can keep it when the service disappears
best_practices: Make the local write authoritative immediately; do not model 'optimistic' and 'confirmed' as different states
Give every write a hybrid logical clock timestamp and a node id so merges are deterministic and idempotent
Persist the outbound operation log durably before attempting any network send
Distinguish 'not loaded yet' from 'empty' in the UI — folding an empty value onto a loading row erases data
Keep CRDT metadata out of undo capture and define a compaction policy for row history
references: Ink & Switch, Local-first software: you own your data, in spite of the cloud, https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/
Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg and McGranaghan, Local-first software — seven ideals and CRDT foundations, https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/local-first.pdf
Automerge, CRDT implementation by Ink & Switch, https://automerge.org/
MDN, Using Service Workers — cache-first and offline-first request handling in the browser, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Service_Worker_API/Using_Service_Workers
